"title": "Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis",

"type_of_paper": "Experimental / Mechanistic Study",
"executive_summary": "This study addresses the limitations of traditional linearized kinetic analyses in electrocatalysis, which often fail to capture complex phenomena like surface coverage effects and mixed control. The authors developed a robotic system capable of sequentially testing up to ten electrochemical cells with varying electrodes, electrolytes, and gas compositions, enabling the collection of large datasets required for cohesive kinetic analysis. Using this platform, they investigated the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to carbon monoxide (CO) at three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). The analysis revealed that these catalysts exhibit non-ideal kinetic behaviors, specifically voltage-dependent changes in bicarbonate and CO2 reaction orders. These complexities were attributed to mechanisms involving electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent degrees of rate control. The study concludes that such complex mechanisms are likely prevalent across this class of electrocatalysts and that automation is essential for uncovering them. The work provides a robust framework for interrogating reaction mechanisms that are not amenable to standard Tafel or order dependence analyses.",

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng; Vineet Padia; Joseph H Maalouf; Aditya M Limaye; Alexander H Liu; Michael A Yusov; Ian W Hunter; Karthish Manthiram
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the limitations of traditional linearized kinetic analyses in electrocatalysis, which often fail to capture complex phenomena like surface coverage effects and mixed control. The authors developed a robotic system capable of sequentially testing up to ten electrochemical cells with varying electrodes, electrolytes, and gas compositions, enabling the collection of large datasets required for cohesive kinetic analysis. Using this platform, they investigated the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to carbon monoxide (CO) at three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). The analysis revealed that these catalysts exhibit non-ideal kinetic behaviors, specifically voltage-dependent changes in bicarbonate and CO2 reaction orders. These complexities were attributed to mechanisms involving electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent degrees of rate control. The study concludes that such complex mechanisms are likely prevalent across this class of electrocatalysts and that automation is essential for uncovering them. The work provides a robust framework for interrogating reaction mechanisms that are not amenable to standard Tafel or order dependence analyses.

claims.description: Automation enables the collection of data necessary for cohesive kinetic analysis in electrocatalysis.
Complex, non-linearizable reaction mechanisms are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts.
Ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in the literature might be reconciled by differences in operating conditions.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the limitations of traditional linearized kinetic analyses in electrocatalysis, which often fail to capture complex phenomena like surface coverage effects and mixed control. The authors developed a robotic system capable of sequentially testing up to ten electrochemical cells with varying electrodes, electrolytes, and gas compositions, enabling the collection of large datasets required for cohesive kinetic analysis. Using this platform, they investigated the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to carbon monoxide (CO) at three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). The analysis revealed that these catalysts exhibit non-ideal kinetic behaviors, specifically voltage-dependent changes in bicarbonate and CO2 reaction orders. These complexities were attributed to mechanisms involving electrolyte poisoning and potential-dependent degrees of rate control. The study concludes that such complex mechanisms are likely prevalent across this class of electrocatalysts and that automation is essential for uncovering them. The work provides a robust framework for interrogating reaction mechanisms that are not amenable to standard Tafel or order dependence analyses.

Research Context
Traditional electrocatalysis relies on linearized rate data. Linear methods assume factorable dependences on voltage and concentration. Complex phenomena like surface coverage violate these simplifying assumptions. Cohesive kinetic analysis offers a more robust alternative for complex mechanisms. However, cohesive analysis requires extensive data collected over wide ranges. Manual data collection for such extensive ranges is time-consuming and prone to error. Existing automation strategies focus on high-throughput screening rather than kinetic analysis. Current screening methods often lack the versatility needed for detailed kinetic interrogation.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can automation enable the collection of data necessary for cohesive kinetic analysis? Do immobilized metal tetrapyrroles exhibit complex, non-linearizable mechanisms? Are bicarbonate and CO2 orders dependent on applied potential? Can phenomena like electrolyte poisoning explain these kinetic behaviors? Do CoPc and CoTPP share a similar mechanism distinct from FePc? Are non-ideal mechanisms prevalent across this class of electrocatalysts?

Methodological Details
Three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts were selected for study. Cobalt phthalocyanine was used as the first catalyst. Cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin was used as the second catalyst. Iron phthalocyanine was used as the third catalyst. CoPc catalysts were dissolved in N,N-dimethylformamide. CoPc was drop-casted onto calcined Toray060 carbon paper. CoPc loading was 5.98 x 10^-11 mol/cm^2. CoTPP and FePc were dissolved in carbon black-containing DMF. CoTPP loading was 5.11 x 10^-10 mol/cm^2. FePc loading was 8.04 x 10^-10 mol/cm^2. Carbon black was added to less active catalysts to increase loading. Electrolytes were prepared from stock solutions of Na2CO3 and NaClO4. Stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO2. Electrolyte solutions had an overall 1 mol/L ionic strength. A robotic system was developed to automate sequential testing. The system can test up to ten electrochemical cells. Each cell can have a different electrode, electrolyte, and gas composition. Electrolyses were queued in batches of ten. All ten runs in a batch used the same electrolyte composition. The reference electrode was a leak-free Ag/AgCl type. The reference electrode was calibrated daily. The reference electrode was swapped every 1-3 days. Data files were automatically uploaded to an SQL database. A python script was used to access files with relevant run conditions. Output included average current and partial currents for CO and H2.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot consists of a single cell body housing reference and counter electrodes. The cell body moves horizontally to sequentially perform electrochemistry. The cell body moves vertically to open and close onto any given cell pan. Electrolyte is pumped through the electrolyte in port on the side of the cell body. Two configurations exist for the electrolyte source: individual vials or common reservoir. In this work, the common reservoir configuration was employed. Gas flow is initiated through the gas in tubing after electrolyte flow. A gas chromatograph is connected to the gas out port for online detection. The cell assembly is analogous to a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell. A carbon paper disk working electrode is clamped between top and bottom cell pans. The working electrode exposes a well-defined 10 mm diameter circle. A 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire serves as the counter electrode. Cell body cleaning is achieved by moving to a wash station. Cleaning involves pumping milliQ water in and out for several cycles. The user loads electrodes, electrolyte, and specifications into an Excel queue file. The robot automates sequential testing as described. Run information and data files are uploaded to the SQL database upon completion. The cycle can be repeated after running the cell body robot wash sequence. This workflow enables queuing up to ten electrolyses for a single effort.

Key Results
Analysis focused on partial current toward CO production. Signatures of mechanistic complexity were apparent in canonical Tafel, CO2, and bicarbonate dependences. Such kinetic signatures have only been reported in one previous work at CoPc. CoPc and CoTPP show voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition. FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. These features can be explained by adsorption of bicarbonate onto an unoccupied catalyst site. CoPc and CoTPP models invoke bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control. FePc mechanism likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. CoPc CO2 order dependence appears quite ideal, within error for first order. CoTPP apparent order in CO2 is slightly below one. CoTPP order appears to slightly decrease at more reductive potentials. CoTPP behavior is characteristic of a model with surface saturation effects. FePc apparent CO2 dependence is perhaps the most unusual. FePc order is more attenuated at less reductive potentials. FePc curves for different potentials intersect. At low CO2 partial pressures, voltage inhibits the reaction for FePc. Signatures of non-ideal reaction mechanisms are observed across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. Two distinct trends are observed for bicarbonate inhibition. Both observations can be explained by mechanisms invoking explicit catalyst poisoning or accumulation of a bicarbonate-dependent reactive intermediate.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Non-ideal mechanisms are likely prevalent across this class of electrocatalysts. Kinetic phenomena such as electrolyte poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed control are important considerations. Ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in the literature might be reconciled by differences in operating conditions. Limited range measurements only see one part of a much more complicated whole. Automation combined with cohesive kinetic analysis provides an informative experimental strategy. Future work could explore incorporation of a membrane to separate anode and cathode. Alternative electrolyte and gas flow configurations could be explored. Software development to automatically enumerate mechanisms could standardize the workflow.

Contradictions And Limitations
Data collected with the automated setup showed rates up to ten times lower than previously reported. Faradaic efficiencies toward CO were lower than expected, typically under 30%. Incomplete Faradaic efficiency closure was observed, with only c.a. 60% attributable to CO and H2. The remaining Faradaic efficiency was presumably lost to oxygen reduction. Relatively high FEs toward HER were observed, typically around 30 to 60%. The one-compartment cell design lacks a membrane, allowing crosstalk. Metal crossover from Pt anodes onto copper CO2RR cathodes has been observed. Currents are below the theoretical mass transport limited current density. Flow configuration can have unexpected influence over measured kinetics. Proposed mechanisms only qualitatively capture the observed trends. The study does not propose a specific reaction mechanism. The study does not discuss kinetic behaviors for CO2RR at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles beyond the initial discussion at CoPc.

Claims
Automation enables the collection of data necessary for cohesive kinetic analysis in electrocatalysis. The system automates sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells. The workflow enables queuing up to ten electrolyses for a single effort. The resulting experimental workflow was more time-and labor-efficient. Manual collection can entail months of intensive yet menial experimentation. Automation can assist with cohesive kinetic analysis.
Complex, non-linearizable reaction mechanisms are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrrole electrocatalysts. Signatures of non-ideal reaction mechanisms are observed across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. CO2 and bicarbonate order dependences are non-linear and/or change depending on the applied voltage. Such kinetic signatures have only been reported in one previous work at CoPc. Traditional analyses assume factorable dependences on voltage and concentration. Kinetic phenomena such as electrolyte poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed control are important considerations.
Ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in the literature might be reconciled by differences in operating conditions. Kinetic measurements reported in a limited range of operating conditions only see one part of a much more complicated whole. The study does not discuss kinetic behaviors for CO2RR at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles beyond the initial discussion at CoPc. Further engineering efforts may improve the throughput and reduce the labor requirements of data collection.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data robustness was evaluated by comparing newly measured rates against literature precedent. Previously reported kinetic trends in CO production were preserved. The newly collected data was well-correlated with that of the previous work. Hallmarks of non-ideal reaction mechanisms were clearly evident in the data.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robotic system enabling flexible and automated reaction rate data collection for heterogeneous electrocatalysis. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation of non-linear and voltage-dependent CO2 and bicarbonate order dependences across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. 3. The future path involves extending the automated system with a membrane and software to automatically enumerate mechanisms.
